items.title: A reaction that gets cold all by itself
items.claim: Mix solid barium hydroxide octahydrate with solid ammonium thiocyanate in a beaker. The mixture turns into a slush and drops to about minus 20 degrees Celsius — cold enough to freeze the beaker to a wet wooden block.
items.prompt: How can a reaction proceed if it absorbs heat from its surroundings?

options.text: It can't — the textbook is wrong
Endothermic reactions only happen when energy is supplied externally
The enormous increase in entropy (two solids becoming liquid and gas) outweighs the unfavourable enthalpy change in the Gibbs equation
The reaction is actually exothermic at the molecular level — the cooling is an illusion

items.reveal_title: Entropy can drive a reaction uphill in enthalpy
items.reveal:
Gibbs free energy: delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. The reaction is strongly endothermic (positive delta H), but it produces 10 moles of liquid water plus 2 moles of ammonia gas from 2 moles of crystalline solid. The entropy change is huge and positive.

At room temperature T delta S is larger than delta H, so delta G is negative — the reaction is spontaneous and proceeds, sucking heat from the surroundings as it does.
items.why: Students learn 'exothermic equals spontaneous' as a rule of thumb. Entropy can outvote enthalpy when disorder rises sharply.

items.title: Industry uses 'wrong' conditions for the Haber process
items.claim: The forward reaction N2 + 3H2 to 2NH3 is exothermic, and it reduces gas moles from 4 to 2. Le Chatelier says: high pressure, low temperature for maximum ammonia yield. Real plants run at 400 to 500 degrees Celsius — warm, not cold.
items.prompt: Why deliberately choose a temperature that lowers the equilibrium yield?

options.text: Cooling the reactor is impossible at industrial scale
The iron catalyst only works above 400 degrees
At room temperature the rate is so slow that even a high equilibrium yield is useless — moderate temperature is a compromise between rate (kinetics) and yield (thermodynamics)

items.reveal_title: Thermodynamics tells you what is possible; kinetics tells you whether it happens this century
items.reveal:
At 25 degrees Celsius the equilibrium for ammonia synthesis is excellent — but the activation energy is around 230 kJ per mol without a catalyst. The Maxwell-Boltzmann tail at room temperature has effectively zero molecules with that much energy. The reaction takes geological timescales.

The iron catalyst lowers the activation energy, and 450 degrees Celsius makes enough molecules energetic enough to react quickly. Yield drops to about 15 percent, but the unreacted gases are recycled. Throughput, not single-pass yield, is what matters.
items.why: Le Chatelier predicts the equilibrium destination. It says nothing about how fast you arrive.

items.title: Gas pressure is molecular hammering
items.claim: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is 101,325 Pa — about 10 N on every square centimetre. That force comes from air molecules hitting surfaces about 10 billion times per second per square centimetre.
items.prompt: Why don't we feel atmospheric pressure crushing us?

options.text: Pressure only acts on hard objects
Pressure pushes equally on all sides; the air inside our bodies pushes outwards with the same force as the air outside pushes in, so the net force is zero
Atmospheric pressure is too small to feel

items.reveal:
Air molecules at room temperature travel at about 500 m/s on average. They collide with any surface — including your skin — about 10 to the 23 times per square metre per second. Each collision exchanges a small momentum; the cumulative effect is pressure.

Your blood, lungs and tissues are at the same pressure as the surrounding air. The forces inside and outside cancel — you feel nothing.

Go to high altitude (low outside pressure) and the inside-outside balance shifts. Air rushes out of sinuses unevenly, ears pop, gases trapped in fillings expand. Rapid decompression in aircraft can rupture lungs if breath is held.
items.why: Pressure feels like a single, distant force. It is the time-averaged result of countless individual molecular impacts.
